title: Adding 1.2 hours of sleep cut daily intake by 270.4 kcal without a diet [sleep_duration_diff, ei_diff_in_changes, free_living_routine]
teaser: In a 4-week trial of 80 adults with overweight, extending sleep by 1.2 hours a night reduced daily energy intake by 270.4 kcal compared with habitual sleep. [overall_mean_age, eligibility_age_bmi_sleep, sleep_monitoring_duration, sleep_duration_diff, ei_diff_in_changes] Look closer, and half of that gap came from the control group eating more. [ei_ctrl_change, ei_ext_change, limit_control_increase]
hook: Most weight trials tell people what to eat or how much to move. [-] This trial gave 80 adults no diet or exercise plan at all and only changed their bedtime. [overall_mean_age, free_living_routine, sleep_extension_target]
populationPanel: Who was studied: 80 adults aged 21 to 40 with a BMI between 25.0 and 29.9 who usually slept less than 6.5 hours a night. [overall_mean_age, eligibility_age_bmi_sleep] All 80 were randomized to extend their sleep or keep their usual schedule for 2 weeks at home. [baseline_and_intervention_periods, free_living_routine] People with sleep apnea, insomnia, or recent night-shift work were excluded. [exclusion_sleep_disorders_shift]

card.question: Does sleeping longer at home reduce how many calories adults eat? [sleep_extension_target, ei_diff_in_changes]
card.headline: Adults who extended their sleep took in 270.4 fewer kcal a day than the control group, relative to baseline. [ei_diff_in_changes]
card.support: Energy burned did not show a clear difference between groups. [tee_diff_in_changes, tee_p_value]

glance.alt: Five horizontal interval bars comparing daily energy intake, energy balance, total energy expenditure, activity expenditure, and fasting metabolic rate between sleep extension and control groups. [ei_diff_in_changes, eb_diff_in_changes, tee_diff_in_changes, aee_day_diff_in_changes, rmr_fast_diff_in_changes]
glance.note: Compare the energy and weight changes inside. [-]

paragraphs: Think of body weight as a two-sided ledger: calories coming in through food versus calories going out through movement and resting metabolism. [energy_intake_method] The trial tracked both sides in real life without asking adults to count calories. [free_living_routine, energy_intake_method]

When adults in the sleep extension group slept 1.2 hours longer a night, their daily energy intake fell while their daily energy burn showed no clear difference. [sleep_duration_diff, ei_ext_change, tee_diff_in_changes, tee_p_value] Across all participants, each 1-hour gain in sleep went with 162.3 fewer kcal eaten per day. [energy_intake_per_hour_sleep]

Because intake dropped and burn stayed steady, adults in the sleep extension group shifted into a lower energy balance and lost 0.48 kg over 2 weeks, compared with a 0.39 kg gain in the control group. [eb_diff_in_changes, wt_ext_change, wt_ctrl_change, baseline_and_intervention_periods] Most of the 0.87 kg gap between groups was fat-free mass rather than fat mass. [wt_diff_in_changes, ffm_diff_in_changes, fm_diff_in_changes] [concept:fat-free-mass]

After 2 weeks of tracking their usual sleep at home, 80 adults were randomized to 2 weeks of sleep extension or continued usual sleep. [baseline_and_intervention_periods, overall_mean_age] The sleep extension group received one-on-one sleep hygiene counseling aiming for 8.5 hours in bed, plus a brief check-in on day 22. [sleep_hygiene_counseling_delivery, sleep_extension_target, day22_followup]

Both groups continued their normal daily routines with no prescribed diet or physical activity. [free_living_routine] Wrist actigraphy tracked sleep continuously for all 4 weeks. [sleep_monitoring_duration, actigraphy_device] Researchers calculated energy intake from doubly labeled water, body scans, and twice-daily hidden home scale weights. [energy_intake_method, dlw_method, body_energy_stores_method, hidden_scale_weights]

audit.effect: Between-group difference in energy intake change (sleep extension minus control): −270.4 kcal/d (P < .001). [ei_diff_in_changes, ei_p_value]
audit.weakEnd: The 95% confidence interval runs from −393.4 to −147.4 kcal/d. [ei_diff_in_changes] Even the weak end, 147.4 kcal/d lower, is a meaningful daily gap over 2 weeks. [ei_diff_in_changes, baseline_and_intervention_periods]
limitations: The control group's energy intake and weight rose from baseline, which contributed to the between-group gap. [limit_control_increase]
The intervention lasted 2 weeks, so it cannot show how long adults can keep up extended sleep. [baseline_and_intervention_periods, limit_short_duration_sustainability]
The doubly labeled water method has a 5% precision limit, adding uncertainty to energy intake estimates. [limit_dlw_precision]
Strict eligibility criteria in adults with overweight limit how widely these numbers apply. [limit_generalizability]
audit.missed: The 270.4 kcal/d gap is a difference of two moves: intake fell by 155.5 kcal/d with sleep extension but rose by 114.9 kcal/d in controls. [ei_ext_change, ei_ctrl_change, ei_diff_in_changes] Also, fat-free mass accounted for 0.62 kg of the 0.87 kg weight difference, versus 0.25 kg for fat mass. [ffm_diff_in_changes, wt_diff_in_changes, fm_diff_in_changes]
more: Total energy expenditure (−53.9 kcal/d, P = .19) and activity energy expenditure showed no clear difference between groups. [tee_diff_in_changes, tee_p_value, aee_day_diff_in_changes, aee_day_p_value]
Fasting resting metabolic rate differed slightly (−32.5 kcal/d, P = .047), while post-meal metabolic rate did not (P = .41). [rmr_fast_diff_in_changes, rmr_fast_p_value, rmr_post_p_value]
Primary outcome data were complete for 75 participants (93.8%), with 90.0% in sleep extension and 97.5% in controls. [complete_ei_data_overall, complete_ei_by_group]
Funded by the National Institutes of Health, with no conflicts of interest reported. [funding_sources, conflict_of_interest]

glossary.plain: Participants were placed into the sleep extension group or the control group by chance, like flipping a coin, so the two groups started out similar.
A motion-sensing watch worn on the wrist that records when a person goes to bed, wakes up, and how long they sleep at home.

takeaways: In adults with overweight sleeping under 6.5 hours, aiming for 8.5 hours in bed added 1.2 hours of sleep and reduced daily intake by 270.4 kcal compared with controls. [eligibility_age_bmi_sleep, sleep_extension_target, sleep_duration_diff, ei_diff_in_changes]
Limiting electronic devices before bed appeared to be a key habit for participants who extended their sleep. [limit_sleep_factors_unassessed]

Weight changed over 2 weeks without any prescribed diet, though most of the short-term difference was fat-free mass rather than fat mass. [free_living_routine, baseline_and_intervention_periods, ffm_diff_in_changes, fm_diff_in_changes]

steps.label: Aim for 8.5 hours in bed tonight
steps.detail: Set a bedtime that gives you an 8.5-hour window in bed, matching the trial's target.

steps.label: Limit electronic devices before bed
steps.detail: Put phones and screens away before sleep, a key habit reported by participants.

steps.label: 8.5 hours in bed on at least 5 nights this week
steps.detail: Consistent longer nights were linked to lower daily calorie intake in the trial.
